newsitem.title: FRANCE: Pragmatic Paris designers shun art for art's sake.
newsitem.headline: Pragmatic Paris designers shun art for art's sake.

text.p: Paris designers came down from their pedestals on Thursday and turned out clothes for the real world, making a break with the intellectual meanderings of the avant-garde and the costume parades of more whimsical minds.

The most successful example of the fourth day of the winter ready-to-wear season was at Kenzo, where the designer married flamboyant ethnic fabrics with sober men's suiting, creating a riot of colour based on Siberian and Japanese influences.
He juxtaposed dustcoats and jackets of dark gabardine, pinstriped wool or pocked tweed over exuberant peony-print kimono silks and gold brocade shawls.
Chapka-coiffed models bundled into snug bouclette coats with plush collars of mink or fluffy Mongolian lamb, or wrapped themselves in multiple layers of long cozy cardigans and horse-hair boots.

The show was about contrast -- a heavy sheepskin jacket over a wispy chiffon dress washed with kimono flowers, a splendid ethnic jacquard sweater on a skirt of masculine pinstripes -- and luxuriant colours of fiery red, fuschia, and deep purple steadied by the strictness of masculine fabrics.

But Kenzo deprived himself of much media exposure when several dozen photographers and television cameramen walked out of the collection in a huff at being squeezed into a corner of the designer's salon.

Earlier, American designer Alber Elbaz presented his first collection for ailing French fashion house Guy Laroche, turning out an unremarkable but highly commercial collection that may be the perfect remedy for the firm's flagging sales.

He did it with dresses and coats of fuzzy mohair in persimmon, cyclamen and turquoise, tailored suits of lacquered chevron tweeds and soft wool jackets, gathered in back for volume, over boyish trousers.

There were also baggy bubble coats, a mink jacket and dress set and a series of long jersey gowns in coffee, pigeon grey and anthracite with backs dipping low to the coccyx and glimmering taffeta ruffles at the hem.
The tailoring was not always what it should have been, but the clothes won't scare away customers with difficult to wear avant-garde styling or theatrical fashion statements.

There was a spark of creativity in cut velvet Renaissance gowns with waistlines high on the ribcage, and irridescent black cocktail wear with a big taffeta bow at the nape of the neck or a flower nestled in a draped back.
